appraisal_events.evidence: Au jugement de Mme Leroi, le salon de Mme de Villeparisis était un salon de troisième ordre; et Mme de Villeparisis souffrait du jugement de Mme Leroi.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Leroi's contemporary verdict brands Mme de Villeparisis's salon as third-rate, and Mme de Villeparisis is reported as genuinely wounded by that judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mais personne ne sait plus guère aujourd'hui qui était Mme Leroi, son jugement s'est évanoui, et c'est le salon de Mme de Villeparisis... qui sera considéré comme un des plus brillants du XIXe siècle par cette postérité.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator decisively reverses the earlier verdict: posterity forgets Mme Leroi and her judgment entirely, while ranking Mme de Villeparisis's salon among the most brilliant of the century.

status_effects.explanation: In the present of the scene, her salon is contemporarily disparaged by Mme Leroi's authoritative social judgment, and she suffers visibly from it.

The narrator's own retrospective verdict reverses the contemporary slight, ranking her salon among the most brilliant of the century by posterity's judgment -- a separate, later moment from Mme Leroi's snub.
The same narratorial reversal erases Mme Leroi's standing: her once-authoritative judgment is said to have vanished, and almost no one remembers who she was.

ambiguities: Mme Leroi's contemporary judgment (E1) is reported as a plain social fact, but it is immediately and retroactively undercut by the narrator's reversal in E2, so E1's stance could also be read as quietly ironized rather than purely neutral.
